studies.title: Cognitive and affective effects of L-Theanine: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 randomized trials
studies.dose: single 200mg dose (primary analysis); repeated dosing up to 400mg/day for 8 weeks in secondary analyses
studies.duration: acute single-dose primary outcome; some included trials up to 8 weeks
studies.outcome: choice reaction time/attention (primary: acute stress); secondary: anxiety, depressive symptoms, fatigue
studies.result: Single 200mg dose 30-60min pre-test significantly improved choice reaction time (SMD=0.51, 95% CI 0.25-0.77). Acute stress reduction was modest (SMD=0.31) and largely driven by high-risk-of-bias studies. No significant effect on fatigue. Anxiety effects were inconsistent/non-significant except one trial (400mg/day x8wk in psychotic anxiety, SMD=0.54). Depressive symptoms reduced after single dose (SMD=0.69, excluding one outlier). No serious adverse events reported.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Acute effects of tea constituents L-theanine, caffeine, and epigallocatechin gallate on cognitive function and mood: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.dose: varied across pooled studies; theanine and caffeine administered alone and combined
studies.outcome: alertness (Bond-Lader), attentional switching accuracy, other unisensory/multisensory attention measures
studies.result: Moderate effect sizes favoring combined caffeine+L-theanine over placebo for alertness and attentional-switching accuracy in the first 2h post-dose. Moderator analysis found caffeine dose was a stronger driver of effect size than theanine dose, particularly in the first hour.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: The effects of L-theanine, caffeine and their combination on cognition and mood
studies.design: randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, balanced crossover RCT (Haskell et al.)
studies.dose: L-theanine 250mg, caffeine 150mg, alone and in combination
studies.outcome: RVIP accuracy, simple/working-memory reaction time, mental fatigue and alertness ratings, delayed word recognition
studies.result: L-theanine alone increased headache ratings and reduced correct serial-sevens subtractions. Caffeine alone improved RVIP accuracy and digit vigilance RT. The combination improved RVIP accuracy, mental fatigue ratings, simple RT, working-memory RT and sentence-verification accuracy beyond either alone, plus a significant caffeine x theanine interaction on delayed word-recognition RT.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Acute effects of theanine, caffeine and theanine-caffeine combination on attention
studies.dose: L-theanine 200mg, caffeine 160mg, combination, black tea, placebo
studies.outcome: recognition visual reaction time (RVRT), simple visual RT, ERP N2-P300 amplitude
studies.result: Mean RVRT significantly improved by theanine (P=0.019), caffeine (P=0.043) and combination (P=0.001), not by tea or placebo. Combination elicited a significantly larger N2-P300 amplitude than theanine alone (P=0.029) or caffeine alone (P=0.005). No significant theanine x caffeine interaction on RVRT or amplitude.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: Anti-Stress, Behavioural and Magnetoencephalography Effects of an L-Theanine-Based Nutrient Drink: A Randomised, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Crossover Trial
studies.design: double-blind, placebo-controlled, balanced crossover RCT with MEG
studies.dose: L-theanine-based nutrient drink (specific mg dose not stated in abstract)
studies.outcome: subjective stress response to cognitive stressor, salivary cortisol, resting-state alpha oscillatory activity (MEG)
studies.result: Subjective stress response to a multitasking stressor was significantly reduced 1h post-dose; salivary cortisol reduced at 3h. Resting-state posterior alpha oscillatory activity was significantly greater 2h post-dose vs placebo, but this effect was only apparent in participants higher in trait anxiety, and was not correlated with the stress or cortisol changes. No treatment-related cognitive performance changes were observed.
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

studies.title: The effects of L-theanine consumption on sleep outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.design: systematic review and meta-analysis (19 articles, 18 in meta-analysis)
studies.population: humans of all ages and health status
studies.dose: varied across included RCTs; authors note a lack of studies on 'pure' L-theanine
studies.outcome: subjective sleep onset latency, daytime dysfunction, overall subjective sleep quality
studies.result: L-theanine significantly but modestly improved subjective sleep onset latency (SMD=0.15, 95% CI 0.01-0.29, n=10 studies), subjective daytime dysfunction (SMD=0.33, 95% CI 0.16-0.49, n=9), and overall subjective sleep quality (SMD=0.43, 95% CI 0.04-0.83, n=12).
studies.fundingConflict: not stated in abstract; not independently verified

verdicts.claim: Calm Focus (Alpha Waves) — evidenceStrength strong, 'robust EEG evidence showing alpha wave increase within 45 minutes, one of the most replicable effects'
verdicts.reason: The only identified human EEG/MEG RCT (White 2016) found increased resting alpha activity at 2h post-dose, not 45min, and only in the subgroup with higher trait anxiety — not a universal, replicable effect as the site's blanket claim implies, and it did not correlate with subjective calm or cortisol change.

verdicts.claim: Anxiety Reduction — evidenceStrength strong, 'significant in both healthy and anxious populations... notable at 200mg and above'
verdicts.reason: The largest and most recent meta-analysis (31 RCTs, 2026) found anxiety effects 'inconsistent and non-significant' except one small clinical trial at 400mg/day for 8 weeks; two earlier 200mg RCTs in healthy adults (Lu 2004 vs alprazolam, Rogers 2007) found no significant acute anxiolytic effect under experimentally induced or baseline anxiety.

verdicts.claim: Sleep Quality — evidenceStrength moderate, magnitude small, 'reduces sleep latency and improves sleep quality ratings, particularly when combined with magnesium'
verdicts.reason: A 2025 meta-analysis of 18 RCTs (n=897) confirms significant but small effects on sleep latency, daytime dysfunction and overall sleep quality (SMD 0.15–0.43), matching the site's 'moderate evidence / small magnitude' rating; the specific claim about combining with magnesium was not found tested in any identified RCT and is unverified.

verdicts.claim: Caffeine Synergy — evidenceStrength strong, magnitude large, 'the combination outperforms either compound alone... the best-evidenced nootropic stack in existence'
verdicts.reason: Multiple independent RCTs (Haskell 2008, Kahathuduwa 2016) and a dedicated meta-analysis (Camfield 2014, 11 RCTs) consistently show the L-theanine+caffeine combination outperforms either compound alone on attention/reaction-time measures; this is one of the better-replicated acute nootropic effects in the literature.

doseAssessment.trialRange: 97–250mg single dose across RCTs (most common: 200mg); chronic sleep trials used 50–900mg/day
doseAssessment.suggestedText: 100-200mg/day is well within the trial range; no change needed. Fix the internal 1:2 vs 2:1 caffeine-ratio inconsistency between the clinicalDose field and the FAQ/stacksWith text (trials like Haskell 2008 and Kahathuduwa 2016 used roughly 1:1 to 1.6:1 theanine:caffeine ratios, not a fixed 2:1).

safetySignals.signal: No serious adverse events reported across a 31-RCT meta-analysis (n=1168); site's 'extremely well tolerated' claim is consistent with the evidence.

gaps: Site's own text is internally inconsistent on the theanine:caffeine ratio (1:2 in clinicalDose field vs 2:1 in FAQ/stacksWith text) — needs a single corrected figure.
No RCT was found testing L-theanine + magnesium specifically for sleep, despite the site's FAQ recommending this combination.

The 'alpha wave within 45 minutes' framing is not supported at that specific timepoint by the one identified EEG/MEG RCT (which measured at 2h, in a trait-anxiety subgroup only) — broader EEG literature search would be needed to confirm or refute a 45-minute effect.
